translations.text: A discourse delivered by Saint Athanasius, archbishop of Alexandria, on the saying written in the Gospel according to Matthew: “The kingdom of heaven is like a rich man who went out early in the morning to hire workers for his vineyard.”
The Lord said in the Gospel of Matthew, “The kingdom of heaven is like a rich man who went out early in the morning to hire workers for his vineyard.”
He agreed with the workers on a stater a day and sent them to his vineyards.
He went out at the third hour and saw others standing idle in the marketplace.
He said to the others, “You too, go to my vineyard, and I will give you what you deserve.”
And they went.
He went out again at the sixth and ninth hours and did the same.
When he went out again at the eleventh hour, he saw others standing there.
He said to them, “Why have you been standing here idle all day?”
They said to him, “Because no one has hired us.”
He said to them, “You too, go to my vineyard.”
So let us now investigate and understand who these workers are, what this vineyard is, and who this master of the house is.
First of all, the lord of the vineyard is God the Father, who has governed his creatures from the beginning.
Speaking with them also through the prophet, he tells us, “The vineyard of the Lord of Hosts is the house of Israel, and the man of Judah is the beloved’s new planting.”
The workers he hired first are Moses, Aaron, and Joshua son of Nun.
He called Moses in the land of Midian, saying, “Come, go down to Egypt and bring my people out of that place.
Work in my vineyard through the commandments, the ordinances, and the decrees.”
He agreed with them on a stater—the honor of being a prophet. For Aaron, in turn, it was the high priesthood over his people. And they went.
Those of the third hour are the judges. He also sent them over his people: “I will give you what you deserve.”
They are not prophets; they are not apostles. Rather, what they deserved was this title: “judges.”
Those of the sixth and ninth hours are Samuel, David, and all the prophets.
Samuel worked in the vineyard with a horn.
David brought a vine out of the land of Egypt. He worked on it with a harp.
Hosea found Israel like grapes in the wilderness. Amos:
He said, “Israel is a fine vine that spreads out, and its fruit is abundant.”
Those of the eleventh hour are the apostles, whom he found idle all day.
These are the ones excluded from all the deeds of lawlessness, whom no one hired. The devil could not persuade them to worship idols.
He could not persuade John the Baptist to go to taverns, places for eating and drinking.
He could not persuade Peter to embrace unbelief.
He could not persuade Andrew to enter a defiled marriage and become a woman's slave.
For this reason they called him Boanerges, which means the son of the thunder of heaven.
For no one on earth could hire them to work for him and pay them according to what they deserved.
For their wages are abundant in heaven.
For this reason the Savior said to all the apostles, “My Father, the people you gave me out of the world—I found them to be chosen vessels.”
“Again, of all those you gave me, I have lost none. And no one can come to me unless my Father, who sent me, draws him.”
Look, these words tell us that it is the Father who hires workers for his vineyard.
Who, then, is this steward?
I say that it is the Lord, Jesus Christ, the Son of God, who holds all the Father's possessions, namely the mysteries.
[?] his powers are present in Israel and the other nations. For he himself said, “The Father loves the Son and has placed everything in his hands.”
He is a son because the inheritance belongs to him.
He is a steward because he is the one who pays the workers, and the whole world is under his authority.
Because he holds the keys of David. He is a vine.
Because he is the one who brings joy to all creation.
He is also bread.
Because he is the one who satisfies all creation.
When evening came, the owner of the vineyard said to his steward, “Call the workers and give them their wages. Begin with the last until you reach the first, and give each one a stater.”

The Father said to the Son, “Whether at the end or during the day, you are the one who knows. Call the workers and give them their wages—all the workers who worked on behalf of the human race—and give them the wages for their work.”
Paul said, “God appointed some in the church: first, the apostles,” whom he began to pay first; second, the prophets, and the rest.
The first came, thinking that they would receive more.
Listen to him. He said, “I tell you that many prophets and kings longed to see what you see, and did not see it.”
The stater he gave them is the apostleship and the holy offering.
He said, “When they received it, they grumbled against the owner of the vineyard, saying, ‘Why
have these last ones worked only one hour, and you have made them equal to us?’”
Who are these who grumbled and envied these last workers, except [?] the scribes and the Pharisees? For they too were sent to work in the vineyard.
These are the ones he cries out against: “Why have you burned my vineyard? And the plunder taken from the poor is in your house.”

For they too received the law through the ordinances of angels, but did not keep it. And they grumbled against the Lord about the disciples of John and those of the Pharisees: “They fast, but yours do not fast.”
“Why do your disciples violate the tradition of the elders?
They do not wash their hands when they are going to eat their bread. They eat, drink, and live in luxury.”
The apostles, for their part, gnash their teeth; they eat because they are hungry. They wander in the world.
These people, in turn, grumble: “Why do your disciples break the Sabbaths?” They envied these last true workers.
He answered and said to one of them, “Friend, I am not treating you unjustly.
Did I not agree with you on a stater? Take what belongs to you and go.”
Who is this who received all these rebukes?
I say that it is no one other than the one who was told, “Friend, do what you have come for.” That is Judas, who attacked the Savior with great grumbling.
“Why was this ointment not sold for three hundred staters and the money given to the poor?”
If you care about the poor, you traitor, why do you steal their belongings from your money box?
“Or is your eye evil because I am good?”
For he was wicked, stealing what was put into it,
while the Savior, for his part, was good to him and patient with him.
But he said to him, “Am I not allowed to do what I want with what belongs to me?”
This is God's defense concerning it: “Am I, God, not allowed to give greater wages to the one who works, and to judge those who act wickedly?”
These are the testimonies, or the grumblings, of Judas. For he grumbled with his tongue,
but he was [?], merciless in his heart.
He is wicked in his soul, a thief with his hands, and shameless in his eyes.
Whenever they ate, the apostles would take care not to put their hands into the bowl before the Savior. They were afraid and said, “Who are we to eat with God?”

But Judas, the insensitive one, would plunge his hand into the bowl with the Savior, eagerly dipping his piece of bread at the same time during the meal, ahead of the Savior, while the Savior said nothing. But so that we might understand,
when the disciples asked him, “Who, then, is going to betray you?”
he gave them the sign of Judas’s insensitivity: “The one who puts his hand into the bowl with me first is the one who will betray me.”
He said to him, “What you are going to do, do quickly.”
For the Savior was eager to complete the salvation of his creation on the cross, according to the will and command of his Father.
Would you find him growing weary, or neglecting what he had come for, or being afraid of death?
But he was showing his courage in facing the cross, as a strong martyr and as a fearless God.
For this reason he urged Judas, “What you are going to do, do quickly.”
“Hurry! But all these created beings are in suspense. They are waiting for you; they are also waiting for me.
Those in heaven are waiting for me. Those in the abyss and chaos are waiting for you.
My Father is with me and helps me. The devil is with you; he stands with you at your right hand and helps you.
The holy angels are crowning me at the gates of heaven. The punishing powers are preparing the things of the underworld for you.”
He urged him with these words: “Hurry, for I am ready for the lashes.”
It is therefore rightly said in Ezra: “Creation is not more eager than the Creator.”
But if Judas is the one who will betray him, why does he address him as “Friend, I am not treating you unjustly”?
Because he said to him, “Your eye is evil, but I am good.”
The Savior did not withhold the expression of his friendship from him, right up to the moment when he betrayed him.
He calls him “Friend,” but he is thinking of hostility.
He gave him the money box, and he became a thief.
He chose him as a disciple, but he was thinking of deceit. He chose him as a human being, and he became a devil.
O Judas, what have you done? What did you gain by betraying the Lord?
You have forfeited your life and lost this great honor, the glory of being an apostle.
For who is above their allotted position? After the designation of angels come the apostles.
For a person scarcely considers his son worthy to eat with him, and a slave cannot eat with his master.
But Jesus our Lord consented to eat with tax collectors, and he drank with Judas the lawless one. A vile man stretched out his hand together with God.
This wretched man forfeited his life because he accepted death for himself. He exalted himself beyond what he deserved; he fell down to the ground as he deserved.
He chose him among the apostles, and he lost his apostleship.
He was appointed an heir, and he deprived himself of the inheritance.
The apostles are the Savior’s heirs. They are the light of the world, but they could not give light to Judas.
They are the salt of the earth, but they could not season Judas's filth.
They are the ones God placed in the church, but they could not make him remain with them.
Because they surpassed the limits of humanity, he came to be on the devil's side.
Woe to you, Judas! What have you gained? Cain, who killed a human being, is better than Judas, who killed God.
Saul, who hated a human being, is better than Judas, who hated God.
Pharaoh's hardness of heart toward the people is better than Judas's hardness of heart toward God.
Balaam's error is better than Judas's lawlessness.
Korah's rebellion in the wilderness is better than Judas's stubbornness in Jerusalem.
Achan, who hid things devoted to destruction, is better than Judas, who hid acts of mercy.
Absalom's arrogance toward David is better than Judas's insolence toward God.
Ahithophel's evil counsel against David—he hanged himself and died—is better than Judas's accusations against the Savior—he hanged himself and ended up in Tartarus.
Shimei's curses against David are better than Judas's mockery of the Savior.
The blood Joab wickedly shed is less than the blood Judas mercilessly shed.
Gehazi's greed, which caused him to become leprous, is better than Judas's greed.
He went to destruction. Jeroboam's sin is less than Judas's lawlessness. Jeroboam made a false god, while Judas cast out the true God.
Friend, I am not treating you unjustly. Take what is yours and go.
Wicked friend, Judas, it was not the Savior who treated you unjustly, but you yourself. Take the curse and go away to the underworld.
Judas came to be in this condition. Matthias came in and received the blessing. He became a disciple at the Teacher's feet.
He became an apostle and preached.
He became a light to the lands.
He became salt and seasoned souls. He became a servant and submitted to the Lord.
He became a son of God's beloved, Jesus Christ, the King of all.
The Lord of all, the pride of all, the one who guides all, the one who will judge all, the one who had compassion on all.
The one who is merciful to all, the one who died for all, the one who rose for all, the one who set all free, the one who transformed all.
The one who made all things new, the one who made all rejoice, the one through whom all grow.
Now then, O human being, come and board the ship of salvation, which is the faith of the church.
It has two oars with which it is rowed. These are the two Testaments. As you study them, they will bring you to the good anchorage.
It has a mast and a yard, which are the cross of the Lord. These are your two hands stretched out in prayer to God.
It has a rudder that steers it. This is the authority of the Lord, which will guide you along every good path.
It has a sail, which is the bishop in the church.
The helmsman steers it. This is Jesus, who steers everything.
It has sailors aboard it. These are the clergy who serve in the church.
Its passengers have boarded it. These are the Christian people.
And you will anchor in the good harbor, which is the landing place of Jesus, which is the heavenly Jerusalem.
And you will inherit God's promises, which are his good things, and you will rest with your fellow citizens, who are the angels and all the saints.
Now then, brothers and sisters, look: we have spent the whole day working through this discourse until we completed the task we undertook.
Now, then, let us give thanks to God and to the Holy Spirit,
who opened the door of the Word for us and put speech in our mouths, so that we might say what the Word has graciously given us for the benefit of our souls and of those who listen to us.
And let us bless the Word, who has graciously given us the Holy Spirit.
He is also the one who said, “When they speak to you, do not worry about what you will say, for you will be given what to say at that hour.
For it is not you who speak, but the Spirit of your Father who speaks within you.”
But let us, for our part, give glory to God, to God the Almighty, who sent us the King, Christ.
Through him we bless and sing hymns to the Father and the Son and the Holy Spirit, the Trinity of one substance, from eternity through all eternity. Amen.
Athanasius, Archbishop.
Athanasius, Archbishop of Alexandria, speaking about mercy and judgment.
The world that forgets God, brothers and sisters, is gripped by the injustice it inflicts on its neighbors and the cruelty it inflicts on the powerless.
As the holy apostle says, “Just as they did not see fit to keep God rightly before them, God handed them over to a corrupt mind, to do what is improper.”
They are filled with every kind of injustice, malice, wickedness, and greed, full of envy, murder, strife, and evil-hearted deceit, gossipers, slanderers, haters of God, and insolent people.
Arrogant, boastful people who seek out evil.
They disobey their parents and are foolish, untrustworthy, stubborn, untrustworthy, stubborn, and merciless.
Those whom God turns toward worshiping him, he also teaches to keep away from evil and to take care to show mercy to their neighbors.
As Isaiah taught us, speaking on God's behalf: “Stop your wicked deeds; learn to do good.”
For the law contains many commands not to harm our neighbors. It also contains commandments about love for humanity and showing mercy to one another.
For if someone abandons one of these, the other is not enough to set that person right.
For someone who does good to the needy using profits gained through injustice is not accepted before God either.
But if he will give nothing from what he possesses—for concerning those who commit injustice and attempt to offer a gift to God,

It is written: “The sacrifice of the ungodly is an abomination to the Lord.” Concerning the merciless person, he says: “Whoever shuts his ears to avoid hearing a poor person will himself call upon God, and God will not listen to him.”
For this reason Proverbs advises us: “Honor God from your honest labor, and give him the firstfruits from the fruits of your righteousness.”
For if you are going to bring God a gift obtained through oppression and robbery, it is much better neither to acquire such possessions for yourself nor to offer a gift from them.
For you are to bring your vowed offering as a holy gift, as it is written: “The vows of the upright are acceptable before him.”
Again, if you acquire possessions through honest labor but do not bring God offerings from which the poor are fed, they will be counted against you as robbery.
As he says through the prophet Malachi: “The firstfruits and tithes are charged against you, and robbery will be found in your houses.”
For we must now combine mercy with justice: acquiring possessions justly, but distributing them mercifully, as it is written: “Keep mercy and justice, and draw near to your God at all times.”
For God loves mercy and justice, so that whoever takes care to show mercy may draw close to the Lord.
Finally, here and now, let each person examine himself.

Let the rich person examine the possessions he acquires, from which he intends to bring gifts to God: whether he has oppressed the poor, whether he has used force against someone weaker than himself, whether he has exploited someone beneath him, using authority instead of righteousness.
For we are commanded to maintain justice and fairness toward our fellow slaves.
Do not practice oppression because you hold authority, or exploit others because you have power. Rather, because you possess the means to exercise authority, demonstrate deeds of righteousness.
For what is there that you lack the power to do?
Rather, you will give proof of your obedience and your fear of God by not transgressing where you have the power to transgress.
But if you are going to take the possessions of the poor and give them to other poor people, you are better off neither plundering nor giving.
Why do you defile your wealth by adding unjust deeds to it?
Why do you make your offering an abomination by attempting to offer it through oppression, using it to show mercy to other poor people?
Show mercy to the person you are oppressing.
Show kindness to that person, and give generously to this one.
Then you will fulfill mercy and justice.

For God does not share in greed, nor is God a partner in the profits of robbers. Nor did he leave the poor to us because he was unable to feed them. Rather, he seeks righteous and humane generosity from us, for our benefit and our good.
Mercy does not arise from oppression, nor blessing from a curse, nor good deeds from tears.

For God speaks when the tears of those who are oppressed move him: “These are the things I hate, the things you do. You cover my altar with tears, with weeping, and with groaning caused by suffering.”
Deeds of this kind are acts of boasting.
They are acts of vanity.
And they exist for the honor of human beings.
They are not done for the sake of honor from God.
For this reason the Lord rightly said: “Do not act so that people will see you.”

But if you are going to give alms knowing that God is aware of it, you will guard yourself against doing it out of greed for more, knowing that you do not please God in this way—the one who watches over us.
Let us give alms in this way, so that we may receive their reward from God.
God gives his good things to those whom he honors.
But he does not honor anyone who is greedy.
It is no benefit to you to offer a gift to God if you cause your brother grief.
He said, “If you come to offer a gift on the altar and remember there that your brother has something against you,
go first and be reconciled with your brother. Then come and offer your gift.”
So remember Zacchaeus the tax collector, who resolved to repay four times what he had defrauded anyone of.
In this way he distributed his possessions among the poor.

For he knew that he wanted Christ to accept him. And Christ does not otherwise accept those who do not reach out their hand to the poor unless they undo their greed for more—the things they took by force.
And in this way the Lord accepted the uprightness of Zacchaeus.
And he said, “Salvation has come to this house today.”
We have said these things to those who give alms but pay no attention to fairness and justice.
We will—we will also speak again to the person who guards himself against committing injustice but neglects mercy: “A tree without fruit is cut down and thrown into the fire.”
And a tree of this kind never pleases the heavenly farmer, who says, “I came looking for fruit on this fig tree, and I found none.”
He ordered it to be cut down, so that [?] waste the soil as well.
Fault is also found with the person who has not given the poor their due, and a threat is made concerning such a person.
He said, “The person who neglects to give the poor their due will cry out to God, and he will not listen to him.”
God said, “For I am merciful.”

For it is a terrible thing and an act against the law to return to glean your harvest, to return to gather grapes from your vineyard a second time, or to glean your olive grove a second time, because these things should be left for the poor.
But if these things were commanded for those under the law, what shall we say about those who are in Christ?
These are the ones to whom the Lord says, “Unless your righteousness exceeds that of the scribes and the Pharisees, you will not enter the kingdom of heaven.”
Therefore, not only from the fields and the income that comes to us, but also from the work of our hands,
the apostle teaches us to give to those who have nothing.
He said, “You [?] good things, so that you may find a way to give to those in need.”
As for the person who wants to follow the Savior, the Lord instructed him to give from all his possessions for the benefit of the poor, and in this way to follow him.
And those who followed him, together with those who are perfect, fulfilled their great and perfect vow of charity.
He commands them to complete their service through material possessions and move on to service through the word and the Spirit.

As for the rest, he commands them to keep giving and sharing what they have, so that through these things they may be found imitating God's love for humanity, showing mercy, giving, and being generous.
For he said, “Give, and you will be given to. Be kind, and you will be treated kindly.”
Through these, moreover, he promised them fellowship with himself.

For these are the ones who stand at the Lord's right hand, those to whom the King will say when he comes, “Come, you who are blessed by my Father, and inherit the kingdom prepared for you since the foundation of the world.
For I was hungry, and you fed me.
I was thirsty, and you gave me something to drink.
I was a stranger, and you welcomed me.
I was naked, and you clothed me.
I was sick, and you visited me.
I was in prison, and you came to me.”
Then the righteous were amazed and said, “Lord, when did we do these things for you?”
He will say to them, “Truly I tell you, insofar as you did it for one of these little ones, the least of them, it was for me that you did it.”
For eagerness toward the saints is devotion toward Christ.
And whoever is eager to help those who belong to Christ is found to be a servant of Christ.
It is not only because he has much, but even if what he has is little, let him offer it.
And if he gives a disciple just a cup of cold water to drink because he is a disciple, truly I tell you, his reward will not be lost.
He gives you, rich man, an opportunity for true freedom.
For through these things you will be found to be God's fellow worker, supporting Christ's soldiers. And you support them willingly, without their forcing you.
But the King of heaven does not force anyone or collect taxes. Instead, he welcomes eager givers, so that by giving they may receive, and by showing honor they may be honored.
And they share temporal things with the poor so that they may be invited into fellowship in eternal things.
Let us remember these things forever, at all times.
And let them be before our eyes and in our souls, so that when we find an opportunity, we do not let it pass us by, nor neglect what is at hand
now and wait for what is coming, lest, while we wait and put the work off, our end overtake us.
May the Lord grant that we be found watchful and bearing fruit, remembering his commandments, prepared for his glorious rest, with no one reproaching us,
through Jesus Christ our Lord, through whom glory belongs to the Father, together with him and the Holy Spirit, forever and ever. Amen.
Athanasius, Archbishop.
A discourse delivered by the holy patriarch, Father Athanasius, Archbishop of Alexandria, concerning the soul and the body.
The word sent from heaven contains no envy. It is ready to strengthen the things of the soul. You too must be ready to receive the power of the word. But the listener is also needed.
For rain from heaven does not produce fruit without the earth, nor does the earth produce a crop without rain from heaven.
In the same way, the listener does not benefit without the one who teaches him, nor does the teacher benefit without the one who listens to him.
The discourse will supply the word, and let those who listen fulfill the task of listening.
For look, the discourse gives its power; you too, without envy, having first purified yourselves of all jealousy, envy, and unbelief, for these are enemies of righteousness.
For jealousy opposes love, and unbelief opposes faith, just as what is bitter opposes what is sweet, darkness opposes light, evil opposes good, death opposes life, and falsehood opposes truth.
Those who are made complete through the power of the adversary are those who have jealousy, envy, and unbelief, hating love and faith. Those who hate these are enemies of God.
For we know, my beloved, that all who are full of jealousy, envy, and unbelief are enemies of righteousness. Therefore guard yourselves against those who are enemies of righteousness.
And take faith and love to yourselves, for through these all the saints have been saved, from the beginning until now.
Therefore show the power of love, not in words alone but in deeds. For the Lord gave himself as a ransom for us all.
For we did not come into being as the whole world came into being through the word of his mouth. Rather, he created us through both word and deed.
God was not content to say, “Let us make a human being according to our likeness and our image.” Rather, he makes the deed follow the word.
For God took some earth from the ground and shaped it into a human being according to his image and likeness. He breathed a breath of life into his face.
But Adam came under the power of death because of his transgression, and Adam's created form needed to be formed again by God the Creator, so that he might be saved.
For the human being lay still, buried in the earth, after the spirit had separated from him—the spirit that he had breathed into him, which had become a breath of life.
So he was held in a dark place when he died, in the place called Hades.
For the soul and the body were divided, and death separated them from one another.
The soul was bound in Hades, while the flesh decomposed in the earth.
And there was a great distance between them, between the flesh and the soul.
The flesh decayed and was scattered in the earth in which it had been buried, while the soul became powerless in the bonds of Hades.
The soul, which was strong, was bound in darkness.
The weak one, the body, decomposed in the earth.
For the body cannot move while it lies decomposed in the mountain, nor can the soul do anything while it is bound in Hades.
For when death took the human being, it bound the strong part—that is, the soul—in Hades, while it dissolved the weak part—that is, the flesh—in the earth.
For just as a tyrant who is about to capture a royal city first seizes the king and holds him firmly under his control,
so death takes the soul first, leaving the body like a ship with no one steering it. This is how the body decayed: it fell apart limb by limb because the soul had stopped steering it.
And the limbs were scattered on the mountain. They decayed like an abandoned city, like a ship with no one steering it that has sunk into the water.
For the soul steers its own body like a king administering his city.

For when the person died, his soul could no longer steer his flesh, because it was bound in the underworld. And it had lost its way on the paths of righteousness, like a pilot whose ship has lost its way at sea.

The soul turned away from the straight paths, and they carried it off onto the robbers’ roads so that they could plunder it there. These are adultery, sexual immorality, love of adornment, idol worship, murder, and hatred.
For these are the things through which the soul destroyed the person.
And because of these he became a corpse in the mountains. But the soul was handed over by the evil one, whom it had followed, to be held captive in the underworld.
For he had plundered it like a robber.
Furthermore, he left it to itself, unable to help its own body, which had decayed.
The flesh came apart in the earth at its joints, and the limbs separated from one another because the soul was not in them to bind them together.
The soul itself is bound in the underworld, not in fetters but in bonds.
Because of this, it could not help its own body to keep it from decaying in the earth.
For just as a pilot dies and his ship goes to ruin,
so too, if the soul had not been bound in the underworld, it would have steered its body to keep it from decaying.
The soul, then, was bound not only with bonds, but also with its own sins as with ropes. Because of this it became powerless and left its body behind, decaying in the earth.
And the soul is also being tormented in the underworld, having become death’s footstool.
It remains in the underworld, weeping and groaning over its beautiful body, saying:
“Where is my body, in which I used to sing—in it—hymns?
Where is my body, in which I used to pray to God?
Where is my beautiful body, in which I used to be a person among my friends and relatives, walking with them in it?
I used to dance in my body. For while I was in my body, they called me a person. But now I am not a person; I am a soul.
For when death separates the soul from the body, it is called a corpse, and it gives off a foul smell.
I was looking for my body; I was not looking for my name—the body with which I used to be a person and in which I used to speak.
For when the soul departs from its body, it does not return to speak in a loud voice, but in a faint and very feeble voice.
Like a musical instrument with no sound, it is speechless.”
This is the condition of the soul when it does not have the body through which to cry out.
For it has decayed in the earth like a broken vessel that has become useless. It has neither voice nor sound. It is motionless, for it is a corpse.
For the soul that used to adorn it has departed. The one who speaks has been taken away from it.
It is impossible to recognize the likeness of anyone who has died, for he has shriveled in the sand.
Nor will you recognize his face, the shape of his body, or his size. Nor will you hear anyone's voice.
For a son will not recognize his own father, or his mother, or his brother, or his friend. It is impossible to recognize his face in the tombs.

His lips have shriveled, his nose has rotted, and his eyes have closed. The color of his face has changed. It is impossible to recognize any of them, because all the bodies in the tombs have become dust. They have decayed, and no remnant of them remains before us.
For we cannot identify a bone so that it can be joined to its own body, because the bone is exposed, with no flesh covering it.
Even before the flesh covering the bone has rotted, you cannot recognize whose it is.
For who has ever recognized a bone from among the limbs?
Or who can tell us the color of someone who has died?
For you cannot recognize Adam's bones, or which are the prophets' bones, or which bodies belong to the patriarchs or the apostles.
They all lie scattered in the earth. Their heads and their bodies lie scattered.
If a son searches for his father, he will not recognize him in the grave, nor will a friend recognize his friend or a brother his brother.
He will not find anyone's name so as to recognize that it is truly that person. Nor will he recognize his appearance, because they have become dust in the grave, with no human form remaining in them.
For humanity is scattered over the face of the whole earth and lies scattered everywhere. The earth is covered with tombs and graves, and every place is filled with the stench of the dead.
The earth itself has become one single grave for the dead.
One single person was taken out of the earth, but thousands upon thousands and tens of thousands upon tens of thousands have been buried in it.
Every place is full of the dead: the sea and the rivers, the earth and the mountains. Wild animals and birds have eaten and drunk from the corpses of the dead.
And Hades has been filled with souls in bonds.
O creation of the earth, so full of sorrow! O human creation, growing only to perish and ending in sorrows and groans!
The joy of those on earth lasts only a short time. Although they think it is great, it quickly vanishes from their grasp.
For look: someone rejoices that he is about to marry a woman, and then he weeps over her when she has died.
Look again: someone rejoices over his children, and then, behold, he weeps over their tomb.
Look again: someone rejoices over his father, and afterward he mourns as they bury him.
For what does a person gain? A person is a sorrow with no consolation in it.
It is impossible to console the one who will perish, nor is there anyone who will comfort him.
He is a man like him; he too dies. What friend will comfort his friend when he himself is also subject to death?
What prophet of God will comfort them? Yet they will not listen to him.
Indeed, they did not believe in the God of heaven, nor did they obey his command, until they fell into death.
For he is still angry with man because of his transgression. The disasters that befall man are unspeakable and indescribable.

For everything treats man violently because of his transgression: sickness, loss, grief, sorrow, and the suffering surrounding him; cold and scorching heat; fire, wild animals, birds, and reptiles; the seasons and old age.
The winds and earthquakes, the rain and dew harm man.
The rivers also drown him. He is also eaten by wild animals, burned by fire, and destroyed by death.
They all despised man when he disobeyed God.
And when he was thrown out of paradise, he came out into this realm full of suffering.
In it are envy, adultery, sexual immorality, and idolatry. For these are the things because of which man died.
All these became death’s accomplices against man, and they armed themselves against him with acts of lawlessness so that death might crush him.
For man has no enjoyment at any time or season.
For when has man ever rejoiced?
Did he rejoice while he was in his mother’s womb?
How could he rejoice, packed into the darkness and her stench, squeezed and cramped on every side in menstrual blood?
But did he rejoice as he came out of the womb?
For he was in even greater danger of dying.
But did he rejoice while he was in his mother’s lap
and drinking milk? How is it that he cries out and weeps?
For someone who is comfortable does not cry out or weep.
But did he rejoice when he was a little child crawling on the ground?
How could he rejoice when he was liable to have an animal come upon him and strike him dead, and his mouth was smeared with dirt and dung from crawling on the ground?
But if he grows into a young man, will he rejoice?
How will he rejoice?
He will not be able to rejoice.
For the state of childhood surrounds him on every side with desires full of danger, and he cannot safely act on them, lest he die a terrible death.
But if he takes a wife and has children, he will rejoice.
How will he rejoice when he is worried about his children, lest they act foolishly?
But when he grows old, how has he found rest?
Will he find rest when the dangers of old age are there?
And the last of all these things is the expectation of death, which eats away at the soul like a fire.
O death, which takes every age group: children and old people, the young and grown adults!
For no age limit has been set for death; instead, it takes every age group. For what becomes of a human being?
For it is a great sorrow to witness a person's death and decay.

The face grows pale in the appearance of death, along with the body that has grown cold, the mouth that is silent, the hair that has become disheveled, the eyes that have clouded over and closed, and the limbs that do not move.

For the remains of the body in the earth—the flesh that has decayed, the muscles that have rotted, the other remains that have been stripped bare, the sinews that have come apart, the veins that have dried up, and the abundant dust—
For a human being is nothing, and is like a flower of grass that dries up and decays, like wood that is burned by fire and consumed.
For after the destruction of the human being and his great misery,
God himself cared for his own creation, which he had made in his likeness and image, so that death would not be victorious
and boast, saying, “I have conquered the human being.”
For the devil wages war against the human being at all times, and he took him captive through the evil of death and the gates of Hades.
He continually hurled his lawless deeds at the human being until he secured him in death’s grasp, and he confined him in the dungeon of Hades.
Because of this, the soul, bound in darkness, could not escape from the places where the dead are laid.
For this reason, the Father sent his Son to the earth without flesh, because he is a holy spirit.

He caused him to become flesh in the womb of the virgin, and God became a human being to save the one who was lost and gather those scattered by the devil’s envy, bringing them together into his flock.
Those whom death had scattered by dividing the human being, Christ gathered together, making the human being one again, soul and body.
For death bound the soul in Hades and dissolved the flesh in the earth, dividing the human being in two.
The Savior Jesus, in turn, freed the soul from its bonds and bound the flesh together again with the sinews.
And he brought both together and made them a single whole, the soul and the body; he joined them to one another.
He gave the body to the soul, and the soul to the body.
He gave the instrument to the speaker; he gave him the appointed limbs.
Now then, O soul, sing in their body [?], since they have their own God, who is inseparable. For this is why Christ died for us: so that we might live with him forever.
For did he owe a death that he had to die?
Or what need was there for him to become human?
Or did he himself need to take on flesh?
He is God, upon whom rests all the glory of divinity.
For this reason he endured the birth of mortal human beings, although he himself is the immortal God.
But why did he come down to earth, when he is the king who reigns over the heavens?
Who compelled him to give his consent to the cross and to die joyfully?
He is the creator of everything, yet he endured being born in a woman's womb and being wrapped in swaddling cloths.
He who is clothed in all the glory of his Father.
He who sits upon the chariots of the cherubim was laid in a manger and received milk from a woman's breast.
He before whom seraphim stand trembling, glorifying his divinity.
He who sends water to flow in the rivers, and who sends rain and dew from heaven, received baptism in the Jordan from a mortal man.
He through whom everything receives light was mocked by the Jews.
He upon whose word the seven heavens, the firmament, the earth, and the underworld hang was hung on a wooden cross.
He who took lifeless earth and shaped it into a living human being endured being mocked, so that through his humiliation he might save the human being who had gone to destruction through his sin.
He gave his soul as a ransom for the souls of human beings.
He gave his holy flesh for the whole creation of Adam, and he gave his blood for everyone.
He gave a human being for a human being, and his death for our death.
For the death that human beings owe and fear has become a blessing, because Christ died for us.
This is the love that Christ revealed when he died for us sinners, so that he might save us.
For what righteous person has ever died for even a single sinner?
Or what father has died for his own son whom he fathered?
And what friend has died for his friend?
Or a beloved brother for his brother?
For no one has ever done this: for one person to die for another by his own will or under his own compulsion.
But Christ himself came of his own free will and out of his love.
We are sinners. Not only did he form us like Adam, making us human,
But when we were ruined by sin, he came and suffered for us, and brought us to life through his love.
for when he formed us with his hand, he did not suffer. But now he has brought us to birth again through the suffering of his death, suffering anguish over us like a woman in labor.

For he was exceedingly patient with us: he did not burn up the world when they humiliated him with whips at the hands of sinners, killing him and burying him, just as the prophet says, “You brought me down into the dust of death.”
Who brought him there?
It was the people of the ungodly, those whom he loved, who killed him.
He came to them to save them, and they struck out like a thorn.
Look, then, O human being, at the humiliations that the children of Israel inflicted on our Lord.
They pierced the side of the one who created them.
They made the one who had done many good things for them and their ancestors suffer.
They repaid good things with evil things, and conceived hatred in place of the love with which he had loved them.
They afflicted the one who had given them joy,
the one who had raised the dead among them while they watched him,
the one who had healed the lame and cleansed the lepers.
The one who had given light to the blind—this is the one they killed and hung on a tree.
Look, then, O people, at the audacity of the Jews.
They hung up the one who had suspended the earth.
They nailed the one who had established the world upon the waters of the seas.
They tore the one who had arranged the heavens in his wisdom.
They bound the one who had freed them from slavery to Pharaoh.
They tied up the one who sets sinners free.
The one who had given them a spring of water and quenched their thirst—they gave him sour vinegar to drink.
And they fed him gall while he was in the agony of death on the cross, not remembering that he had given them honey to drink from a rock.
They bound the hands and feet of the one who had freed those held captive, bound by the devil because they had done his will.
He held them captive under his power until the one who would redeem the captives came and released those who were bound.
The one who sends the sun and the moon to shine on them—the one who opened the eyes of the man born blind—they closed his eyes as though he were asleep.
They buried the one who raised the dead.
Oh, this new and incomprehensible mystery!
They judged the judge.
They bound the one who forgives their sins.
They put nails into the hands of the one who formed them.
They hung up the one who breathed their breath into their nostrils.
They tore apart the one who will tear apart the limbs of their body.
[?] The one who nourished the earth with food—they forced him to eat bitterness.
The one through whom everything lives died. For they did not insult him only on the cross, but even before he died they hurled terrible insults in his face.
When our Lord was hanging on the wood of the cross, the tombs opened and Hades split apart.
He rescued the souls. He raised the dead. Many of the saints appeared in Jerusalem.
And before the mystery was completed on the cross.
For when Christ died, he crushed the enemy. He bound the powerful tyrant. He set his cross upright, standing firm before them and bearing victory.
For our Lord Jesus Christ raised his body on the cross, and when death saw life, it fell beneath his feet.
Then the powers of heaven marveled at his wisdom.
The angels gazed down at him.
The elements were afraid, and your whole creation was shaken when they saw this new mystery and this terrifying spectacle.
They saw God hanging at the hands of human beings, as they lifted him up on a wooden beam.
His feet were fastened to it with nails.
His hands likewise were stretched out, as they drove the nails into the wood.
The Jews, for their part, mocked him, laughing and jeering. But they did not understand the mystery.
The earth trembled when it saw the shamelessness of the Jews.
The mountains swayed; the hills were shaken and moved.
The sea raised its waves so as to cover the world.
The abyss shook and opened its mouth to swallow you all.
Creation shook with anger at the insolence of the defiled Jews.
The lights of heaven became dark. The sun set. The moon shook and hid itself. The stars ceased shining so that they would not give light to the ungodly.
The moon was full of light, yet it did not shine when the sun set. Instead, they were all in darkness.
As they saw their God, who had created them, hanging on a tree like a robber.
The day became dark.
An angry angel came out from among all the angels, with his sword drawn in his hand, slaughtering them ten thousand by ten thousand at once.
And when they were restrained by the mercy of Christ,
he turned to the curtain of the temple and tore it, splitting it in two from top to bottom.
All the angels were looking out from heaven in anger, since the patience of God the Father had restrained them all from destroying them.
The daylight fled and left the world in darkness—dense darkness.
All these things happened before Christ closed his eyes.
And his light hurried and shone in Hades.
Hades shook when the Lord descended into it, not in the flesh but in the spirit.
For he held everything back, lest it perish before its time.
He poured his blood onto the earth and protected the earth and everything in it.
His body remained hanging on the cross for the sake of the elements, while his spirit descended into Hades and saved those who were there.
He plundered Hades and took control of everything.
His body raised the dead on earth, while his spirit freed the souls in Hades.
For at the time when our Lord's body was hanging on the cross, at that very time the tombs opened.
The guards of Hades saw him, trembled, and fled.
He smashed the bronze gates and shattered the iron bars, and he brought their souls, which were in Hades, up to his Father.
For when the Lord destroyed Hades and trampled on death, he made the enemy a laughingstock.
He brought the souls up from Hades and raised the bodies out of the earth.
Look, then, at the astonishing strength of his dead human body as it hung on the cross.
For creation could not bear his dead body, nor could the elements bear him.
For Hades could not withstand his spirit.
For every place is filled with turmoil over the sufferings of our Savior.
And all creation was shaken by his death, for they could not bear to see their Lord being mocked.
All creation tore itself apart, saying, “What is this new mystery?”
“The judge is being judged, and he does not speak.
They see the one who cannot be seen, and they are not ashamed.
They seize the one who cannot be seized, and he does not fight with them.
They despise the one whom they cannot equal, and he does not become angry.
The one who cannot suffer is suffering, and he is not angry.
The one who cannot die has died, and he has endured it.
The one who dwells in heaven has been buried in the earth, and he remains silent.”
“What is this mystery?” said all creation, for they all marveled at his acts of mercy.
And when he rose from the dead early on Sunday, when he trampled on death,
he bound the tyrant and set humanity free.
Then all creation understood that it was for humanity’s salvation that they had judged the judge, and that it was for humanity’s sake that they had seen the invisible one.
They measured the immeasurable one. The one who cannot suffer suffered. The one who cannot die died. They buried the one who belongs to heaven.
For he became human, and they judged him so that he might have mercy on us.
They killed him so that he might release those who were bound.
He suffered so that he might give us rest.
He died so that he might give us life.
They buried him so that he might raise us up.
If the Lord had not suffered as a human, how could humanity have been saved?
Then death fell beneath Christ’s feet, and he dragged it away as a trembling captive. Hades and its power retreated,
having heard the Lord’s voice calling to all the souls, “Come out, you who are bound!
You who sit in darkness and the shadow of death, the light has dawned upon you.
I proclaim life to you, for I am the Christ, the Son of God.”
Then he released the holy souls and raised them up with him.
The earth, in turn, cried out, saying, “Spare me, Lord, and free me from the curse that is upon me, and remove the devil’s wickedness from me.
Because you made me worthy to have your body buried within me in place of the blood they poured out upon me, so that you might raise them up.
For they have scattered your honored image everywhere.
Yet if you had merely said it with your word, no one could have opposed your command. But your love compelled you to come to your creation.
For look, you have stood upon the earth, searching for the members of your creation.
Take the human being for yourself as a trust.
Take back your image, which you buried in me.
Take Adam back, whole as he is.”
Then Christ rose from the dead on the third day and took the saints up with him to his Father.
For all humanity will be saved because of Christ’s death.
For it was one person who was condemned, and the whole world was saved, and mercy was shown to the whole world.
Again, it was one person who died so that they might all rise.
And the Lord died for everyone so that everyone would rise with him.
For when he died, he clothed himself with the human being and took him up with him to heaven and the heavens, being one with him.
He took him as a gift to his Father.
It was not gold or silver, but the human being whom he had made according to his likeness and his image.
This one, then, the Father exalted.
He seated him at his right hand on the exalted throne, and appointed him judge of the living and the dead, and commander of his entire creation.
He who created the heavenly Jerusalem sits upon the cherubim; he is the true bridegroom and the king of all ages.
Glory to him forever and ever. Amen.
Athanasius, Archbishop.
